Alabaster Box
AL-uh-bas-ter BOKS
noun
From the Greek alabastron, a flask or cruse of alabaster — a soft, translucent stone quarried in Egypt and worked into narrow-necked vessels which kept costly ointment from spoiling; the neck was sealed and had to be broken to pour.

Biblical Definition

An alabaster box is not a chest but a flask — a slender vessel cut from soft white stone, sealed at the neck, in which precious ointment was kept from the air. Because the neck was broken to pour, the flask could be spent but once; the giving was total by the very make of the thing. Three times a woman brings such a box to Christ. In the house of Simon the Pharisee, “a woman in the city, which was a sinner… brought an alabaster box of ointment” (Luk 7:37), and washed His feet with tears. In Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman “having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious… brake the box, and poured it on his head” (Mar 14:3; Mat 26:7). She did not measure a portion and cork the rest for another day. She broke it. Nothing was reserved, and the whole house was filled with the odour. The objection came at once, and it came from the disciples: “To what purpose is this waste?” (Mat 26:8). Judas priced the ointment at three hundred pence and spoke of the poor. But our Lord defended her: “she hath wrought a good work on me… she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.” The broken flask was a preaching of the broken body. What is poured out on Christ is never waste; it is the only spending that heaven records, and He promised her memorial wherever the gospel should be preached.

Webster 1828 Definition

A flask of alabaster stone holding precious ointment, sealed at the neck and broken to pour; the vessel of extravagant worship at Bethany.

ALABASTER BOX, a cruse or flask of alabaster, a soft white translucent stone.

Such vessels preserved costly ointments from the air.

The narrow neck was sealed, and had to be broken before the ointment could be poured.

A woman brake such a box upon the head of Christ at Bethany (Mar 14:3).

A woman that was a sinner brought one to His feet in the Pharisee’s house (Luk 7:37).

Key Scripture

Mat 26:7 — "There came unto him a woman having an alabaster box of very precious ointment, and poured it on his head, as he sat at meat."

Mar 14:3 — "And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head."

Luk 7:37 — "And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster box of ointment,"

Mat 26:8 — "But when his disciples saw it, they had indignation, saying, To what purpose is this waste?"

Modern Corruption

The utilitarian objection — “to what purpose is this waste?” — still reckons costly worship a squandering better spent elsewhere.

expand to see more

The corruption is spoken in the text itself, and it wears a benevolent face: “To what purpose is this waste? For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor.” It is Judas’s arithmetic, and the age has learned it by heart. Whatever is spent on the worship of God — the hours, the substance, the beauty, the best of a life poured out with nothing kept back — is arraigned as inefficiency, and a ledger is produced to prove that it might have done more good elsewhere. John notes that Judas said this not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief; and the modern calculus that reduces the church to a distributor of relief and calls adoration wasteful is very often the same heart, with a better reputation. Christ has never yet accepted the objection.

Mark the answer, for it settles the account. “Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me.” The poor ye have always with you, but Christ was going to His burial, and she alone had understood it. Her worship was not a subtraction from mercy but the fountain of it: no man loves the poor rightly who has not first broken his flask over the head of Christ. And the flask had to be broken — there is no pouring while the neck is sealed and the ointment safe. A worship that costs nothing and risks nothing and reserves the remainder for a better occasion is not worship at all. The Lord took her deed into the gospel itself, that wherever it is preached, this also should be told for a memorial of her.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a sealed flask of alabaster stone, broken open to pour out precious ointment.

expand to see more

Alabaster — Greek alabastron, a flask cut from soft white stone.

The stone was quarried in Egypt and worked into narrow-necked vessels.

The sealed neck kept costly ointment from spoiling.

To pour, the box had to be broken — the gift could not be halved.

At Bethany the woman brake the box on Christ’s head (Mar 14:3).

Usage

"She brake the box: the neck must be broken before the ointment can be poured."

"“To what purpose is this waste?” is Judas’s arithmetic, and Christ overruled it."

"What is poured out upon Christ is never waste; He wrote her memorial into the gospel."
